source.title: Scalable Marginal Likelihood Estimation for Model Selection in Deep Learning
source.authors: Alexander Immer; M. Bauer; Vincent Fortuin; Gunnar Rätsch; Mohammad Emtiyaz Khan

record.file_problem: The supplied text contains the full paper and appendix; no material truncation or garbling is apparent.
record.tranche_reason: It compares test performance across architectures and reports width-related trends using test accuracy and marginal likelihood, rather than the original versions’ exact recipes and measures.
record.gate_note: The paper also cites prior claims about flatness and generalization; those citations are not this study’s results. Figure 6 reports a generalization-gap comparison, but exact values are available only in the figure, so the row records the stated qualitative result.
record.test_reason: The study directly compares CNN and fully connected test accuracy under gradient training with online prior-precision optimization, bearing on V3. Its width experiments do not establish widening beyond the zero-training-error threshold required by V2.
record.authors_conclusion: The record is broadly accurate. The authors conclude that scalable approximate marginal likelihood can select architectures and optimize hyperparameters using training data alone, with competitive predictive performance. Their tested CNNs outperform MLPs in the fixed-architecture comparisons, and ResNets outperform standard CNNs on CIFAR-10. Marginal-likelihood rankings generally align with test performance, although on FashionMNIST they sometimes favor smaller models over slightly more accurate ones.
record.recipe_differences: The paper trains image classifiers with online marginal-likelihood optimization of per-layer Gaussian prior precision, then compares test accuracy across architectures. It does not use the claim versions’ exact training recipes.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset and architecture change the relative test performance; the CNN versus MLP and ResNet versus CNN comparisons are dataset-specific.

fits_no_version.finding: On CIFAR-10, ResNet-20 reaches 85.82±0.13% accuracy versus 80.17±0.29% for the standard CNN.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Residual convolutional architectures can outperform standard convolutional architectures under the tested training recipe.

fits_no_version.finding: Wider CIFAR ResNets generally improve test accuracy; narrower FashionMNIST MLPs perform better. No zero-training-error threshold is reported.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Width-performance trends depend on architecture and dataset under online prior-precision optimization.

record.code_released: https://github.com/wiseodd/last_layer_laplace (not stated in the supplied text); the paper links an implementation for Fixup at https://github.com/hongyi-zhang/Fixup
record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), PMLR 139, 2021
record.problems: The architecture comparisons use marginal-likelihood-optimized prior precision, so they do not establish the stated unregularized recipe. Only a subset of the version’s image datasets is tested. The CIFAR-100 width trend is described in aggregate and the cited figure does not provide recoverable individual width-sweep values in the supplied text.
record.rows_left_out: No rows extracted for V2: its width-sweep evidence is summarized as an aggregate trend in Section 4.3 and Figures 2 and 7, without individually recoverable model-condition results. Figure 6’s generalization-gap comparison is qualitative and figure-only; its text says the baseline has a significantly worse negative log likelihood while the test error rate matches, but this does not directly test a named version.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and its coexistence with natural-label generalization.

Whether further widening lowers test error after zero training error is reached. The width sweeps report no interpolation threshold, use optimized explicit regularization, and do not establish training to convergence.

The contribution of local connectivity, learned sparse connections, convolutional initialization of fully connected networks, and CNN-versus-fully-connected comparisons on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and SVHN.
Controlled adaptive-optimizer versus SGD comparisons and tuning-dependent differences.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Dropout interventions and joint removal of dropout and weight decay.
Magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness, its association with generalization gaps, and comparisons with norm and margin measures.
Removal of memorized training examples and retraining.

missing.what: CNN-versus-MLP test accuracy under KFAC-GGN: MNIST 99.46±0.01% versus 98.38±0.04%; FashionMNIST 92.06±0.10% versus 89.83±0.14%. These are additional approximation conditions supporting V3.
missing.locator: Tables 2 and C5; Table A1 confirms the MNIST CNN value.

missing.what: CNN-versus-MLP test accuracy under diagonal GGN: MNIST 99.35±0.02% versus 96.86±0.04%; FashionMNIST 91.69±0.09% versus 85.36±0.21%.

FashionMNIST architecture sweep trained with SGD for 250 epochs: MLP accuracies span 85.01–86.81%, while CNN accuracies span 85.25–93.40%. Larger-performing CNNs exceed every tested MLP, but the smallest CNNs overlap the MLP range; retain architecture sizes and depths when extracting comparisons.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source for these versions. V3 does not require an unregularized recipe, so optimized Gaussian priors do not disqualify its architecture comparisons. Cross-validation comparator results attributed to Immer et al. (2021) are cited results, not additional results of this study. The record incorrectly says individual width-sweep values are unavailable: Tables C9–C11 provide them, but they still do not establish V2's post-interpolation condition.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence are not tested.

The paper varies widths and reports a qualitative width trend, but does not isolate widening beyond the zero-training-error threshold or test the stated unregularized one-hidden-layer ReLU setup on MNIST and downsampled CIFAR-10. The width sweep results are described at an aggregate level and are not extracted as individual model rows.
No CIFAR-100 or SVHN comparison; the paper does not isolate local connectivity as the mechanism or test learned sparse local connections or convolutional initialization.
No comparison of adaptive optimizers with SGD for held-out performance.
No large-batch versus small-batch comparison under fixed epoch budgets.
No dropout intervention or comparison of removing dropout and weight decay together.
No magnitude-aware sharpness measurement or comparison with norm- or margin-based measures.
No memorized-example removal and retraining experiment.
